title: Bolívar and the Liberation of South America

cards.h: Five nations from one man's dream
cards.b:
Simón Bolívar led the wars that freed much of Spanish South America. The modern countries of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia all owe part of their story to him. Bolivia takes its name from him.

Bolívar was a soldier and a thinker. He wanted a united Latin America. His dream failed, but his ideas still shape how Latin Americans think about freedom and unity.

Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783 to a rich creole family, Spanish-born settlers' children born in America. A popular story says that in 1805, on a hill in Rome, he swore an oath to free his country. The story is often told, but its details are uncertain.

He had seen the French Revolution and read Enlightenment writers. He came home determined to end Spanish rule and build a republic.

In 1810 Caracas rebelled, and in 1811 a republic was declared. It collapsed in 1812 after an earthquake and royalist attacks. In 1813 Bolívar issued a decree of "war to the death" against Spaniards who would not join the cause.

The war was brutal. Both sides killed prisoners and civilians. Bolívar fled, returned, lost and won again, and he kept fighting until his victories changed the map.

Simón Bolívar, Carta de Jamaica (1815)

Writing from exile in Jamaica, Bolívar analysed the future of Spanish America. He argued that the region was divided by race, class and geography, and that it would need strong leaders and a new political system.

The letter is one of the most important political texts of the age. Its predictions about division proved partly right.
His great victories came in 1819 to 1824. By the time he died in 1830, most of Spanish South America had won independence.

In 1819 Bolívar led an army of about two thousand men over the freezing Páramo mountain passes to the plains of New Granada. The march was hard, and many soldiers died of cold and exhaustion.

At Boyacá the army surprised the royalists and won a decisive battle. The victory opened the way to Bogotá and made Bolívar the leader of the northern revolution.

Bolívar is often shown as a democrat who believed in freedom for all. Statues and speeches make him a model of liberal hope.

Historians argue that his views were more complex. He admired the British constitution but also wanted strong executive power. His constitution for Bolivia in 1826 gave a president for life, which many saw as a route to dictatorship.

In 1822 Bolívar met José de San Martín, the liberator of Argentina and Chile, at Guayaquil. What they discussed is still debated, but San Martín soon withdrew from public life and left Bolívar to finish the war.

The meeting shows how the wars of independence were led by rival generals as well as by armies. Historians still study it to understand the politics of the time.

Bolívar created Gran Colombia, a union of Venezuela, New Granada and Ecuador, in 1819 to 1822. The union was strained by rivalries between regions and between military leaders. It broke apart in 1830.

Bolívar was ill and exhausted when he died in 1830 on the coast of Colombia. He left a legacy of unity that many Latin American leaders tried to recall, but his union did not survive him.

Bolívar became the Liberator in the minds of many people. Monuments, poems and national holidays turned him into a symbol. Later leaders in Venezuela and elsewhere claimed his name for their own causes.

Historians argue about how to remember him. Some see a hero who freed a continent. Others see a general who fought a civil war and ruled as a strong man. Both views are part of the story.

In 1818 the British had ended the Third Anglo-Maratha War and taken much of central India. The East India Company was building an empire of its own on the subcontinent just as Spanish America was breaking away.

Britain also gained from Latin American trade. British merchants and volunteers helped the independence wars, and the British Legion fought in Bolívar's army. Two empires, two sets of wars, one global economy.

Five things to remember
  1. Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783.
  2. The Jamaica Letter of 1815 analysed Spanish America's future.
  3. He won at Boyacá in 1819 and at Ayacucho in 1824.
  4. Gran Colombia broke up in 1830.
  5. Bolivia is named after him.
Think about it
  • Can a continent be united by a single leader's dream?
  • Was Bolívar a democrat, a dictator or both?
